D009-D008_h001.question:
I’ve been struggling a lot lately—this past year has been the worst. Most days I feel heavy, like nothing matters. I don’t even enjoy grooming the animals anymore, and that used to be the only thing that really made me smile. I’m so tired all the time, even just deciding what to eat wipes me out. Some days, the thought of not waking up feels like a relief.  

But before that, about a month ago, it was the complete opposite. I felt unstoppable. I’d work late into the night, grooming dogs way past closing, talking so fast my coworkers kept asking me to slow down. I’d pace around the salon, couldn’t sit still even for a minute. I’d only sleep a few hours and feel completely wired. My mood swung like crazy—one minute laughing about nothing, the next snapping at customers over small things.  

It wasn’t just a burst of energy—I lost control once. I got into a screaming match with a client, started rearranging the entire grooming station at 2 a.m. without reason. The owner had to call the police because I wouldn’t stop. That’s when they took me in for a few days to calm down. I thought I was fine, but they said I needed help.
D009-D008_h001.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h002.question:
I’ve been feeling so down for about a year now—just empty, like nothing matters. I don’t care about the things I used to take pride in, even getting letters from my grandchildren doesn’t lift my spirits like it used to. I’m tired all the time; even folding laundry feels like too much. Some days, the thought crosses my mind that it’d be easier if I weren’t here—no plan, just… a whisper that won’t go away.

But before this sadness settled in, there was a month where everything was the opposite. I was cleaning the house at 3 a.m., rearranging furniture, calling old friends out of the blue, talking and talking without stopping. My daughter said I was “like a different person”—up and down, laughing one minute, snapping over small things the next. I didn’t need sleep—felt fine on two hours, like my body was buzzing. I paced the living room for no reason, couldn’t sit still.

It wasn’t until I fell while rushing to fix a shelf at night that my son insisted I come in. I didn’t think I needed help, but he said I’d lost weight, looked exhausted. The doctor asked if I’d been hearing voices—no—but I’ll admit, during that high time, I did think God was guiding me, telling me I had a special purpose. That’s not normal, is it?
D009-D008_h002.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h003.question:
I’ve been married for over twenty years and have driven subways underground for the past sixteen—same route, same quiet rhythm. But about a year ago, things started shifting. At first, it felt good—really good. I wasn’t tired, even after only three hours of sleep. I’d wake up buzzing, ideas racing, and start calling old friends, coworkers, even distant cousins just to chat or plan meetups. I felt unstoppable—joking, laughing, like the life of every conversation. I didn’t need rest; I didn’t need much of anything. That lasted nearly a month, and honestly, it didn’t hurt my job. If anything, I felt sharper.

But then it crashed. Out of nowhere, I couldn’t get out of bed. Just crying some mornings—for no reason, or maybe for every reason. Work became a drag; even the controls in the cab felt heavy. I stopped returning calls. The thought crossed my mind: *What if I just didn’t wake up?* I never made plans to do anything about it—never would—but that whisper stayed. The sadness grounded me for months. It’s been a year now. The truth is, nothing’s been *normal* in a long time.
D009-D008_h003.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Bipolar II Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D009-D008_h004.question: There were times—about a month straight—where I felt like I was running on pure lightning. But then it crashed. For over a year, it’s been like I’m underwater. I don’t feel joy, anger, nothing—just empty. I stopped going to the bar with the guys, barely talk to my wife. Thinking wears me out by noon. Sometimes, standing on a balcony during a call, I get this sharp urge to just step off—no plan, just… pull. I never act, but it scares me. That manic month didn’t wreck my job, but this depression? It’s destroying my marriage, my work. I had to take leave. I’m not who I was.
D009-D008_h004.options:
